analysis.one_liner: Makes mining companies pay royalties and cleanup bonds for minerals taken from federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have imposed the first-ever royalties on gold, copper, and other hardrock mining on federal land, died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action after its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Under an 1872 law, mining companies can take gold, silver, copper, and other hardrock minerals from public land without paying the government anything, and old mines are abandoned across the West still leaking acid and heavy metals into water. This bill would have changed that: it would charge a royalty of 2 to 5 percent on what companies pull out, require permits and cleanup bonds before mining starts, and create a fund, paid by a new reclamation fee on mining, to clean up abandoned mine sites in Western states and on tribal land. The bill went nowhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who own the federal land and currently get nothing for the minerals taken from it; people who live near the hundreds of thousands of abandoned hardrock mines in Western and Plains states and on tribal land, where old tunnels and waste piles continue to pollute streams and groundwater; and the states and tribes that would receive money from the new reclamation fund to clean them up.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: Charges mining companies a royalty of at least 2 percent and up to 5 percent of gross income for hardrock minerals taken from federal land, which currently yields no royalty at all, and deposits the money in a reclamation fund [S2][S3].

Creates a Hardrock Minerals Reclamation Fund financed by mining royalties, fees, and a new abandoned mine reclamation fee of 0.6 to 2.0 percent of production value, to pay for cleaning up land and water damaged by past mining, including treating acid mine drainage and protecting public health and safety [S3].
Stops the government from giving away full title to mining claims under the 1872 patent system, except for the small set of applications already on file before the patent moratorium [S2][S3].

Requires exploration and mining permits, public comment, annual inspections, and financial assurance (bonds) big enough to actually cover reclamation and long-term water treatment, so taxpayers are not left holding the cleanup bill [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies, which would for the first time pay royalties on what they extract from federal land, plus per-claim and per-acre fees, an abandoned mine reclamation fee of up to 2 percent of production value, and bonds sized to cover the real cost of cleanup and long-term water treatment. Existing mines already operating were exempted from the royalty, so established producers would have paid least. Some added cost could show up in mineral prices or in projects that no longer pencil out.

drawbacks.text: Existing mines already approved and producing on the day of enactment would owe no royalty at all, and new royalties would apply only going forward, limiting how much revenue the bill would actually raise [S3].

The 2 to 5 percent royalty range is set by regulation and could be set low, and the Secretary is given authority to reduce royalties further for operations that claim production would not otherwise occur [S3].

Requiring exploration permits, hydrologic assessments, reclamation plans, and full-cost financial assurance before any disturbance would add time and cost to opening a mine, and the bill's own reporting provisions acknowledge the royalty and fees could affect domestic mineral exploration and production [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the ledger is lopsided: the public owns the land and the minerals, currently collects nothing, and is left paying for water pollution from abandoned mines that will outlast any company. The costs fall on a specific industry, and the strongest honest objection — that new royalties, fees, and bonding could make some domestic mining projects uneconomic or push production abroad — is real but modest against a 2 to 5 percent royalty with exemptions for existing mines. The bill was not perfectly designed (existing mines escape the royalty, and the royalty floor is low by federal-lease standards), but its death cost the public far more than its passage would have cost miners.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee never took the bill up after its referral, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Udall introduced the Hardrock Mining and Reclamation Act of 2017 in the Senate on September 19, 2017, joined by four Democratic cosponsors: Senators Heinrich, Bennet, Wyden, and Markey [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, the only action it ever received [S5].

The committee never held a hearing or markup and the Senate never voted on the bill; the action history shows nothing after the referral for the rest of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies are better off: they continue to extract gold, copper, and other minerals from federal land without paying any royalty, without new reclamation bonds, and with old mines still free to pollute at the public's expense. Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines continue to bear the cleanup costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining companies still mining federal land royalty-free

for.name: Sen. Tom Udall
for.role: Sponsor; Chairman, Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Interior and Environment
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose royalties, permitting, and reclamation requirements on hardrock mining on federal land.

for.name: 4 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to expire at the end of the 115th Congress.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Gold, copper, silver, and uranium producers operating under the 1872 Mining Law
against.what_they_did: Long opposed hardrock royalties and reclamation bonding mandates as threats to domestic mineral production.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired Energy Committee never gave the bill a hearing or vote, so the fight never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, copper, silver, uranium)
industries.note: The bill would have ended the industry's century-and-a-half-old arrangement of paying nothing for minerals taken from public land: it imposed a 2 to 5 percent royalty, annual maintenance and per-acre land fees, an abandoned mine reclamation fee of up to 2 percent of production value, and reclamation bonds covering real cleanup and water-treatment costs. Existing producing mines were exempted from the royalty, softening the hit to established operators.

The bill would have created a dedicated fund, financed by royalties and a production fee, to pay for reclaiming abandoned mine sites and treating acid mine drainage — paid work cleaning up land and water the public currently owns the liability for.

industries.industry: Mining claim holders and prospectors with small holdings
industries.note: The bill replaced annual assessment-work requirements with a $150-per-claim maintenance fee but waived the fee for holders of 10 or fewer claims who could show they performed the work, sparing hobby-scale prospectors most of the cost while ending the ability to hold claims for speculation.
